cls: Live attenuated mycobacterial immunotherapy / antineoplastic (intravesical) and tuberculosis vaccine
pharm: A live, attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis (Bacillus Calmette-Guerin); when instilled into the bladder it provokes a local nonspecific immune and inflammatory response that has antitumor activity against superficial bladder cancer, and when given intradermally it serves as a vaccine that induces cell-mediated immunity against tuberculosis.
quick: Intravesical: 1 reconstituted vial in ~50 mL saline, retained ~2 h
Avoid intravesical/vaccine use in pregnancy (live organism)
No specific adjustment; topical bladder therapy
Caution; treat disseminated BCG/hepatitis with anti-TB therapy
No direct interaction; avoid hepatotoxins if on anti-TB drugs
Cystitis/systemic BCG infection, fever, sepsis; biohazard handling
summary: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) is a live, attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis used in two main settings: as intravesical immunotherapy for non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (treatment and prophylaxis of carcinoma in situ and prophylaxis of recurrent stage Ta/T1 papillary tumors after transurethral resection), and as an intradermal vaccine against tuberculosis. Instilled into the bladder, it triggers a local immune/inflammatory reaction that destroys residual tumor cells. Because it contains live mycobacteria, it must be prepared, handled, and disposed of as a biohazard, and it carries a boxed warning for the risk of BCG infection ranging from localized irritative symptoms to disseminated, sometimes fatal, BCG sepsis. It must not be given subcutaneously or intravenously, should not be instilled when there is active urinary infection, gross hematuria, or traumatic catheterization, and is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients.
indications: Intravesical treatment and prophylaxis of carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the urinary bladder
Intravesical prophylaxis of primary or recurrent stage Ta and/or T1 papillary bladder tumors following transurethral resection (TUR)
Active immunization against tuberculosis (intradermal BCG vaccine) in selected high-risk individuals (per national immunization policy)

dosage.c: Bladder carcinoma in situ / papillary tumor prophylaxis (induction)
dosage.d: 1 vial reconstituted/suspended in approximately 50 mL preservative-free saline, instilled and retained for about 2 hours
dosage.n: Begin 7-14 days after biopsy/TUR; do not inject SC or IV

dosage.d: 1 vial in ~50 mL saline as per maintenance schedule
dosage.t: Periodic maintenance instillations (e.g., at intervals over months) per protocol
dosage.n: Follows induction; schedule per urology protocol

dosage.d: Per product/strain-specific reconstituted dose (commonly 0.05 mL in infants, 0.1 mL in older children/adults)
dosage.n: Strictly intradermal; follow national policy and product instructions

admin: Prepare, handle, and dispose of BCG as a biohazard using aseptic technique; reconstitute in a separate area away from preparation of parenteral drugs to avoid cross-contamination

For bladder cancer, instill via urethral catheter under gravity, then have the patient retain the suspension for about 2 hours, repositioning periodically; never inject subcutaneously or intravenously
Do not instill within 7-14 days of TUR/biopsy, with traumatic catheterization, gross hematuria, or active urinary tract infection
After voiding, disinfect the toilet (e.g., with bleach) for several hours as the urine contains live organisms
For the vaccine, give strictly intradermally per the product and national schedule; do not give IM, SC, or IV
moa: BCG is a live, attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis. When instilled into the bladder for cancer, it attaches to the urothelium and tumor cells via fibronectin, is internalized, and provokes a robust local nonspecific immune response: recruitment of macrophages, neutrophils, and T cells, with release of cytokines (e.g., interleukins, interferon-gamma, TNF) that mediate a Th1-type cytotoxic, antitumor effect against residual superficial bladder cancer. As a tuberculosis vaccine given intradermally, the live attenuated organism elicits cell-mediated immunity (sensitization of T lymphocytes and macrophage activation) that provides partial protection against serious forms of tuberculosis such as miliary TB and tuberculous meningitis, particularly in children.

absolute: Immunosuppression / immunocompromise (congenital or acquired, including HIV, immunosuppressive therapy, high-dose corticosteroids) - risk of disseminated BCG infection
Active tuberculosis or untreated current TB infection
Concurrent febrile illness, urinary tract infection, or gross hematuria (for intravesical use)
Within 7-14 days of bladder biopsy/TUR or after traumatic catheterization (intravesical)
Known severe hypersensitivity to BCG or any component
relative: Prior severe BCG reaction or BCG sepsis
monitor: Irritative voiding symptoms and severity of cystitis
Fever and systemic symptoms suggesting BCG infection/sepsis
Signs of disseminated BCG (pneumonitis, hepatitis, granulomatous disease)
Biohazard handling and disinfection of urine
Bladder cancer response on surveillance cystoscopy

preg: BCG is a live attenuated organism and is contraindicated in pregnancy; it should not be administered to pregnant women. Women of childbearing potential should avoid pregnancy during intravesical BCG therapy.
lact: It is not known whether BCG components are excreted in human milk; safety during breastfeeding has not been established. Avoid use during lactation unless clearly necessary.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is established for intravesical therapy, which acts locally in the bladder. If disseminated BCG infection occurs and antitubercular drugs are needed, adjust those agents for renal function.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is established. BCG can cause granulomatous hepatitis as part of disseminated infection; such complications are treated with antitubercular therapy, and hepatotoxic interactions of those drugs should be considered.

major: Immunosuppressants and bone-marrow suppressants (corticosteroids, chemotherapy, calcineurin inhibitors, radiation) - impair the immune response, reduce efficacy, and increase the risk of disseminated BCG infection
Antimicrobials with antimycobacterial activity (e.g., fluoroquinolones, isoniazid, rifampin, doxycycline) - may inactivate the live organism and reduce intravesical efficacy
moderate: Other live vaccines - immune interference considerations
minor: No relevant CYP450-mediated pharmacokinetic interactions (biologic agent)
interactions.alcohol: No direct interaction; avoid hepatotoxins (including significant alcohol) if antitubercular drugs are used to treat a BCG complication.
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause a positive tuberculin skin test (PPD) and may affect interferon-gamma release assays; document baseline TB testing status.

serious: BCG infection/sepsis (BCGosis) - high fever, rigors, hypotension
Disseminated BCG with pneumonitis or granulomatous hepatitis
Severe cystitis with reduced bladder capacity
emergency: High fever (>=39.5 C) or fever persisting >48 hours - possible BCG sepsis
Hypotension, rigors, signs of septic shock
Severe systemic illness suggesting disseminated BCG infection

monitoring: Voiding symptoms and severity/duration of cystitis after each instillation
Body temperature and systemic symptoms - persistent or high fever may signal BCG infection
Signs of disseminated disease (respiratory, hepatic, joint, vascular)
Surveillance cystoscopy and cytology for bladder cancer response
Strict biohazard handling and disinfection of voided urine
Anti-TB therapy response if a BCG complication is treated
counsel: After bladder treatment, try to hold the medicine in your bladder for about 2 hours, then sit to urinate to avoid splashing
For 6 hours after treatment, disinfect the toilet by adding household bleach to the bowl and letting it sit before flushing
Burning, frequent urination, and a little blood in the urine are common in the first day or two
Get medical help urgently for a fever of 39.5 C or higher, shaking chills, fever lasting more than a day, or feeling very unwell
Drink plenty of fluids after treatment
Tell every clinician you have had BCG - it can make a TB skin test positive
pk: Local immune/inflammatory response develops over hours to days after instillation; antitumor benefit over weeks
Local cytokine/immune response peaks within days of each instillation
Not applicable - live organism, cleared by local immune response
Induction over 6 weeks; protective/maintenance effect over months
Refrigerate at 2-8 C, protect from light; use promptly after reconstitution; handle as biohazard
pearls: BOXED WARNING and BIOHAZARD: contains live attenuated mycobacteria - prepare/handle/dispose as biohazard and never give SC or IV
Risk of BCG sepsis - persistent or high fever after instillation needs urgent evaluation and antitubercular treatment; do not re-instill during active infection
Contraindicated in immunocompromised patients, during pregnancy, with active UTI/gross hematuria, and within 1-2 weeks of TUR/traumatic catheterization
Avoid antibiotics with antimycobacterial activity (e.g., fluoroquinolones) and immunosuppressants around instillation - they can inactivate BCG or blunt its effect
As a vaccine, BCG protects mainly against severe childhood TB (miliary TB, TB meningitis) and can render the tuberculin (PPD) test positive
Often absent from openFDA structured data - dosing/handling follow the FDA package insert (e.g., TICE BCG) and national immunization guidance
missed: Instillation/vaccination schedules are determined by the treating clinician. If a scheduled instillation or vaccine dose is missed or delayed (for example because of infection or fever), contact the care team to reschedule - do not attempt to make up doses on your own.
overdose: Overdose corresponds to excessive local or systemic exposure to live BCG, manifesting as severe cystitis or disseminated BCG infection/sepsis. There is no specific antidote; management is multidrug antitubercular therapy (e.g., isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol - BCG is typically resistant to pyrazinamide), corticosteroids for severe hypersensitivity/granulomatous reactions, and intensive supportive care for sepsis.
